listening.title: Joining a community sports centre
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký thẻ hội viên trung tâm thể thao
listening.context: A woman phones a community sports centre to register for a membership.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a community sports centre to register for membership. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 8.

script.t: Good afternoon, Ashcombe Community Sports Centre, Daniel speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'd like to sign up for a membership, if that's possible over the phone.
Yes, of course. I can take your details now, and then you just pop in to collect your card. Can I start with your name?
Sure. It's Joanna Caulfield.
Could you spell the surname for me, please?
Yes, it's C, A, U, L, F, I, E, L, D.
Thanks. And what is your address, Ms Caulfield?
It's 42 Linnet Road. That's Linnet like the bird – L, I, N, N, E, T.
Lovely. And that's here in Ashcombe?
Yes, just behind the library, near the primary school.
Great. And a contact phone number?
My home phone doesn't really get used any more, so my mobile is best.
Let me read that back to you. 0, 7, 7, 3, 4 – 5, 9, 2, 6, 1, 8?
That's right.
OK, so what kind of membership were you thinking of?
Well, I was going to get an individual one, just for me. But my son is eleven, and he really wants to come too.
In that case, a family membership might be better value. It covers two adults and up to three children.
Oh, right. Yes, let's go for the family one, then. My husband might use it as well.
How much does that cost? Your website said forty-five pounds a month.
That's the standard family rate, which lets you come in at any time of day.
But if you only use the centre during off-peak hours, it's thirty-eight pounds a month.
And off-peak is when, exactly?
Before five o'clock on weekdays, and all day at weekends.
That suits us fine. I work from home, so I'll go for the off-peak one.
Good choice. And when would you like the membership to start?
Could it start on the 13th of March?
Oh no, sorry – that's the week we're away visiting my parents. Let's say the 15th, not the 13th.
No problem at all. The 15th of March it is.
Now, is there any particular activity you're most interested in? It helps us plan our classes.
I used to swim a lot, but these days it's mainly badminton. I play with a friend from work.
Great, we have courts free most mornings. And finally, how did you hear about us? Was it online?
No, actually. Someone put a leaflet through my door last month, and it had all the prices on it.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 9 and 10.

script.t: Right, that's the form done. When you come in for the first time, you'll need to bring a couple of things.
Do you need proof of address? I've got a bank statement somewhere.
We don't need that, because you're paying by direct debit and the bank checks it.
But we do need a passport-sized photo for your membership card.
OK, a photo. I can do that. Anything else?
No, that's all. Now, you mentioned your son. Is he interested in anything in particular?
He was hoping to try the junior swimming course.
I'm afraid that's full until the summer. But we've just opened a climbing wall.
There's a free taster session for under-fourteens on Saturday morning. I'd really recommend that.
Oh, he'd love that. What about football? He's mentioned your summer camp.
Bookings for that don't open until May, so I'd start with the climbing.
Perfect. Thanks so much for your help, Daniel.
My pleasure. See you on the 15th.

items.cue: Let's say the 15th

listening.titleVi: Tham quan khu chợ cổ được trùng tu
listening.context: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a restored nineteenth-century market hall.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a restored market hall. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Wendlebury Market Hall. My name's Kirsty, and I'll be showing you around today.
Before we start walking, I'll give you a bit of background, and then some practical information about what you can see and do here.
The whole tour takes about forty minutes, and there'll be plenty of time for questions at the end, so don't be shy.
The hall was built in 1868, and it's one of the few covered markets of its kind still standing in the region.
A lot of visitors assume it was a fish market, because of the cold stone floors and the drains you can still see.
But in fact, it was built for the wool trade. Farmers brought fleeces down from the hills every Tuesday.
And merchants travelled from all over the country to buy them. For about fifty years, this was the busiest building in town.
Fish was sold here later, from around the 1920s, but only ever in one corner of the hall.
By the 1980s, the building was in a terrible state, and for nearly twenty years it was closed to the public.
Then a local trust raised the money to restore it. The original plan was to finish the work in three years.
Well, as often happens with old buildings, it ended up taking five, and we finally reopened two years ago.
People often ask me what the hardest part of the job was. You'd probably guess the glass roof, since it's so huge.
But actually, the roof panels were fairly simple to replace. The real challenge was the iron columns holding everything up.
Each one had to be taken down, repaired by hand and put back exactly where it came from, and some of them were badly cracked.
Now, one small request. The floor tiles near the main entrance are original, and they're quite fragile.
You're very welcome to walk on them, and to take photos, but please don't wheel heavy bags or pushchairs across them.
There's a ramp to the right of the entrance that you can use instead.
The tiles were made in a local factory that closed long ago, so if one breaks, we simply cannot replace it.
OK, so let me tell you about the different parts of the hall and what's on offer.
First, the clock tower. You can climb right to the top, and the view across the river is wonderful on a clear day.
But the staircase is narrow, so we only take groups of eight, and you'll need to reserve a place at the information desk beforehand.
Next, the café, which is in the old weighing room. It's open every day from nine, and it normally stays open until six.
On Fridays, though, it closes at three, because the room is used for evening events.
Then there are the craft workshops, where you can watch local weavers and potters at work, and even try a little yourself.
Some people think you have to book these, but you don't. Just bear in mind that they only run on Saturdays and Sundays.
The history gallery is something we're very proud of. It used to be on the ground floor, by the main doors.
But it's now upstairs, in the east gallery, where there's more space and better light for the displays.
If you've got coats or bags you'd like to leave, there are lockers beside the toilets.
Normally they cost a dollar coin, but if you show your entry ticket at the desk, you can use one without paying.
And finally, for anyone with little ones, there's the play corner near the old fish stalls.
It's got soft flooring and small wooden stalls the kids can play shop with, so it's ideal for under-fives.
The lift to the upper floor is being repaired at the moment, by the way, but that should be finished next week.
Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start with those columns I mentioned earlier.
Oh, and one last thing – the gift shop by the exit sells wool from local farms, which seems fitting, given the history of the place.

listening.title: Food waste in university canteens
listening.titleVi: Dự án nghiên cứu lãng phí thức ăn ở căng tin
listening.context: Two students, Maya and Oliver, discuss the draft of their research report with their tutor, Dr Haines.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Oliver, talking to their tutor about their research project on food waste in university canteens. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, you've sent me the draft of your food waste report. How are you feeling about it?
Pretty good, I think. It's been a lot more work than we expected, though.
Yeah, the data collection alone took ages. We were weighing bins every day for three weeks.
Let's go back to the beginning for a moment. Remind me why you chose university canteens as your focus.
Well, I worked in the canteen here in my first year, so I'd seen how much food got thrown away.
That was part of it. But the main thing was that when we searched the literature, there was almost nothing on universities.
Loads on schools and hospitals, but hardly any studies of student canteens. So it seemed like a real gap.
That is a good justification. Make sure you state it clearly in the introduction.
We will. We also thought it would be easier to get access, since we could just ask the catering manager here.
Yes, and that's a perfectly sensible practical reason, but it's not the one to lead with.
And what did the waste audit itself show? Was there anything you didn't expect?
Definitely. I'd assumed the biggest problem would be meat, because it's the most expensive thing they serve.
But it was actually the vegetable side dishes. Students would take them with the set meal and then leave most of them on the plate.
Interesting. And by weight, that was the largest category?
Yes, by quite a long way. Meat was only third, after bread.
Now, your student survey. I think it's a useful part of the project, but there's one problem with it.
Is it the number of people? We only got about two hundred responses.
No, two hundred is perfectly adequate for a project of this size. And the questions were nicely neutral.
The issue is that you only handed out the questionnaires at lunchtime. Students who eat in the evening might behave quite differently.
Oh, that's true. The evening crowd is mostly postgraduates, and they tend to eat bigger meals.
Exactly. You don't need to redo the survey, but you should mention it as a limitation in your discussion.
You also looked at changes the canteens tried out during the term. Which ones did they actually test?
So, the first was taking away the trays. The idea is that if you can't carry so much, you don't take so much.
And the second was an app where students could order their meal in advance, so the kitchen knew how much to cook.
Didn't they also talk about using smaller plates?
They discussed it, but the new plates didn't arrive in time, so that never happened.
And there were going to be posters about waste, but the students' union said no to that.
And charging for second helpings?
That was never really an option. Second helpings already cost extra here.
OK, let's go through the sections of the report one by one. I've made some notes.
The introduction is fine in terms of content, but it's far too long. You could easily cut it by half.
And the literature review? I was a bit worried about that one.
No need. It's very well organised – you've grouped the studies by theme, which makes it easy to follow.
What about the methodology?
That's where I'd like more. At the moment, a reader couldn't repeat your study.
Explain exactly how you weighed the waste, and at what times.
We put all the daily figures in the main text. Is that too much?
It is. The tables are useful, but they interrupt the reading. Put them at the end, in an appendix, and just refer to them.
And the results section? We worked really hard on the writing there.
And it shows – the style is good, so leave that as it is.
But the comparison between the three canteens would be much clearer as a graph or a chart.
OK, that's really helpful. We'll get started on those changes this week.

listening.title: Green roofs in cities
listening.titleVi: Mái nhà xanh trong đô thị
listening.context: A lecture on how cities use green roofs to manage heat and rainwater.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how cities use green roofs. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're looking at green roofs, and why more and more cities are encouraging them.
We'll cover what they are, how they help with heat and with rainwater, and finally some of the problems they bring.
So, first, what exactly is a green roof? Basically, it's a roof that's partly or completely covered with plants.
But you can't just put soil on top of a building. The most important layer is a waterproof membrane, which protects the structure underneath.
Above that, there's usually a drainage layer, then a growing medium – a kind of lightweight soil – and finally the plants themselves.
Broadly speaking, there are two main types. Extensive green roofs have a very thin layer of soil, often less than fifteen centimetres.
Because of that, they're usually planted with sedum, a small plant that stores water in its leaves and survives long dry periods.
Grasses are sometimes used as well, but they tend to struggle in a hot summer.
Extensive roofs are relatively cheap and light, which is why they are by far the most common type on existing buildings.
Intensive green roofs are quite different. They have deep soil and can support shrubs and even small trees, rather like a park.
They look wonderful, but they need regular maintenance – watering, weeding, pruning – just like any garden at ground level.
Let's turn now to heat. You've probably heard of the urban heat island effect.
That's the fact that cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, especially at night.
Dark roofs absorb a huge amount of sunlight and release it as heat. Green roofs reduce this in two ways.
The plants do provide some shade, of course. But the main cooling effect comes from evaporation.
As water leaves the soil and the leaves, it takes heat with it, in the same way that sweat cools our skin.
The difference can be dramatic. On a hot afternoon, a conventional roof might reach seventy degrees Celsius.
Studies have found that a green roof can bring the surface temperature down by as much as thirty degrees.
That's thirty – not three, as it's sometimes misquoted in the newspapers.
And this affects the people inside, too. Top-floor rooms stay cooler, so there is less need for air conditioning.
For building owners, that means lower electricity bills, which is often the argument that persuades them.
The second big benefit concerns rainwater. In a city, most surfaces are hard – roads, pavements, roofs – so rain cannot soak into the ground.
During heavy storms, the drains simply cannot cope, and the result is flooding in the streets.
A green roof acts a bit like a sponge. It holds a large part of the rain and releases it slowly, which reduces that risk considerably.
There is a further advantage. The water that does run off is cleaner, because the soil and roots work as a natural filter.
They trap dust and some of the pollutants that would otherwise end up in rivers.
Green roofs also support wildlife. Ecologists have recorded bees, butterflies and other insects on roofs many storeys high.
Birds visit them too, but much less often than you might expect.
Some researchers now design roofs specifically for wildlife, using a mix of local wild flowers rather than a single plant.
So, why doesn't every building have one? Well, the biggest problem is weight.
When the soil is soaked with rain, a green roof can be extremely heavy, and many older buildings were never designed to carry that load.
They may need expensive strengthening before a green roof can be installed.
Leaks are another worry for owners, although with a good membrane they are actually quite rare.
Cost is an issue as well, of course, but prices are falling as the technology becomes more common.
In our next session, we'll look at some of the policies cities have introduced to overcome these problems.

items.explain: Phòng tầng trên mát hơn nên ít dùng điều hòa, nghĩa là “lower electricity bills” cho chủ tòa nhà. “Lower” được diễn đạt lại thành “reduced”.

items.explain: Nước chảy ra sạch hơn vì “the soil and roots work as a natural filter”. Câu hỏi dùng “act as” thay cho “work as”.

items.text: Wildlife: habitat for bees, butterflies and other ___
items.cue: butterflies and other insects
items.explain: Các nhà sinh thái ghi nhận “bees, butterflies and other insects” trên mái nhà. Bẫy: “Birds” cũng được nhắc nhưng “much less often”, và không khớp với cụm “bees, butterflies”.

items.cue: the biggest problem is weight
items.explain: “the biggest problem is weight” (= main problem), nhất là với các tòa nhà cũ không được thiết kế để chịu tải đó. Bẫy: leaks (rò rỉ) và cost (chi phí) là các vấn đề phụ.

listening.title: Booking a weekend photography course
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký khóa học nhiếp ảnh cuối tuần
listening.context: A woman phones a photography school to ask about a weekend course for beginners.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a photography school to ask about a weekend course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.

script.t: Hi there, Lakeview Lens Studio, this is Dan. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm interested in one of your weekend photography courses.
Great. We've got a few running this autumn. Do you know which one you're after?
I think it's the one for beginners. Something about landscapes?
Right, that'd be Outdoor Basics. It's aimed at people who've just bought their first proper camera.
That's me. My husband gave me one for my birthday and, honestly, I've no idea what half the buttons do.
Then you're definitely in the right place. Let me take a few details first, OK?
Sure.
Can I get your full name?
It's Rachel Thornbury.
Could you spell the last name for me?
Yes, it's T, H, O, R, N, B, U, R, Y.
Thanks. And what’s the best number to reach you on?
Got it. And can I ask how you heard about us?
Well, I picked up one of your leaflets at the library, but actually it was my neighbour who recommended you.
She did a course with you last spring and loved it.
Oh, that's nice to hear. I'll make a note of that.
OK, so about the course itself. Outdoor Basics runs on a Saturday and Sunday, from nine thirty until four.
And when is the next one?
The next one with spaces is the weekend of the 18th of October.
Oh, I'm away that weekend, unfortunately. Is there another one after that?
Let me look. There's the 25th… no, sorry, the 25th is completely full.
After that, the next one starts on the 1st of November. There are three places left.
The 1st of November is perfect. Can I have one of those?
Sure. Now, one thing people often get wrong: the course doesn't start at our studio.
Because it's an outdoor course, everyone meets in the car park at Hollins Reservoir.
Hollins? How do you spell that?
H, O, L, L, I, N, S. It's about ten minutes' drive from town.
OK. And what does it cost?
The standard charge for the weekend is one hundred and sixty pounds.
Oh. That's a bit more than I was expecting.
Well, if you have a library card, we give a discount, so it comes down to one hundred and forty-five.
Oh, I do have one, yes.
Great. And that price covers lunch on both days, plus a framed print of your best picture at the end.
Oh, that's a lovely idea.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.

script.t: Is there anything I need to bring? I was wondering about a tripod.
No need for that, we've got plenty to lend. And camera batteries usually last all day.
But the weather up by the reservoir changes really fast, so definitely bring a waterproof jacket.
Right. And who will be teaching?
Your tutor is Maria Costa. People often ask if she's written books – she hasn't.
But she spent fifteen years taking pictures for a local newspaper before she started teaching.
She's been shortlisted for a couple of national prizes, too, though she hasn't won one yet.
She sounds great. So, can I pay by card now, over the phone?
I'm afraid we can't take card payments over the phone at the moment.
You can do a bank transfer, or bring cash on the first morning.
I'd rather not carry that much cash around. I'll do the transfer this evening.
Perfect. I'll email you our bank details and a map right now.
Thanks so much, Dan. Bye!

listening.title: Shore Keepers coastal clean-up
listening.titleVi: Chương trình dọn dẹp bờ biển
listening.context: A local radio presenter interviews a volunteer coordinator about a beach clean-up programme.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking on local radio about a coastal clean-up programme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 13.

script.t: Good morning. Joining me in the studio is Helen Marsh, who coordinates the Shore Keepers programme here on the Westcombe coast. Welcome, Helen.
Thanks for having me.
For listeners who haven't come across you before, what exactly does Shore Keepers do?
Put simply, we organise volunteers to clear rubbish from our local beaches. But it's also about getting people to notice what ends up in the sea.
And how did it all begin?
So, a lot of people assume Shore Keepers began because tourists complained about the state of the beaches.
And we did get a few letters from visitors, that's true. But what really got us going was the huge storm three winters ago.
It left the whole of Pebble Bay covered in plastic, and a handful of us just went down with bin bags the next morning.
In that first year we had about forty regulars. These days there are over three hundred people on our mailing list.
Of course, not everyone comes every time. On a typical clean-up day, around a hundred and twenty people turn up, which is fantastic.
Now, people keep asking what's changed this year. Well, we're still working on the same four beaches, and we still meet on Saturdays.
The big new thing is that we're asking everyone to record what they pick up, using a simple app on their phone.
That way the council can see exactly where the rubbish is coming from – fishing gear, takeaway packaging, and so on.
It only takes a few seconds per item, and last month alone we logged nearly nine thousand pieces of litter.
That is a staggering number.
Let me run through this month's schedule, because each beach is a bit different.
All sessions run from ten until one, and you can come for an hour or stay for the whole morning – whatever suits you.
We start on the 8th at Pebble Bay. There's a big car park at the top, so getting there is easy.
But there's a steep path down to the sand, and it gets slippery, so please wear proper shoes.
On the 15th we're at Gull Point. Parking's fine there too. It's part of a nature reserve, though, so please leave your dogs at home.
They disturb the seabirds, even on a lead.
Then on the 22nd it's Sandown Cove. That's the easiest of the four – it's flat and sheltered.
So it's ideal if you want to bring the kids along. Under twelves just need to stay with an adult.
And finally, on the 29th, Harbour Beach. The car park there is closed for repairs, so I'm afraid there's nowhere to leave a car.
And the buses don't go that way on Saturdays, so walk or cycle if you can. The toilets are open, at least!
What about equipment and safety? What should people know before they come?
We hand out gloves, sacks and litter pickers at the start, so you don't need to buy anything. Wellington boots aren't necessary either.
But you will need sun cream and a hat. Even in autumn, the sun reflecting off the water is surprisingly strong.
Our safety rules are pretty simple. First, never pick up needles or broken glass yourself.
Mark the spot with a stick and tell a team leader – they have special containers for that.
Second, stay away from the rocks at the far end of each beach. They look solid, but they're covered in weed.
And finally, always check the tide times. The team leader announces them when we start.
When you hear the whistle, everyone moves back up the beach – no exceptions.
And what happens to everything you collect?
Anything that can be recycled goes to the depot in Westcombe. Old fishing nets are sent to a company that turns them into furniture, which people love hearing about.
There's no need to register in advance. Just turn up at the meeting point on the day, and sign in with your team leader.
Helen Marsh, thank you. If you want to join, details are on our website.

listening.title: Feedback on a presentation about bicycles
listening.titleVi: Nhận xét bài thuyết trình về lịch sử xe đạp
listening.context: A tutor gives a student feedback on her presentation about the history of bicycles and urban transport.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear a tutor and a student, Chloe, discussing her presentation on the history of bicycles. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Come in, Chloe. So, I wanted to go over your presentation from Tuesday before you start the written report.
Thanks. I was pretty nervous, so I'm not sure how it came across.
Honestly, it went well. Your old photographs were lovely, and the timeline was clear, but neither of those was what really stood out.
It was the way you opened – with that statistic about factory workers commuting by bike in the 1930s. That grabbed everyone's attention immediately.
Oh good. I almost cut that bit.
Well, I'm glad you didn't. It gave the audience a reason to care about the rest of the talk.
I found it in an old newspaper archive, actually. It took ages, but it felt worth it.
Did you have any particular difficulties preparing it?
Not with the research, really – the library had loads of material. And the slide software was fine.
My real problem was on the day. I was given twelve minutes and I think I took nearly sixteen.
Yes, I noticed. That's something to practise. Now, the section on the safety bicycle.
I did rehearse, but only in my head. I think when you're actually speaking, everything takes longer.
That's very common. Next time, try a full run-through out loud with a timer, and decide in advance which slides you can skip if you're behind.
That's a good tip. I'll do that.
You explained the chain drive and the equal-sized wheels very thoroughly. Perhaps a little too thoroughly.
What was missing was why it mattered for cities – that ordinary workers could suddenly live further from the factory, for example.
Right, I see. I got a bit carried away with the engineering side.
And then you talked about the decline of cycling after the war. What was your main argument there?
Well, most people say it was simply because cars got cheaper. And that's part of it.
But the sources I read argued that the bigger factor was that planners redesigned streets around motor traffic, so cycling just felt dangerous.
Good – that's a more interesting point, and you should make it more strongly.
Some of the audience didn't quite follow it, because it came right at the end when you were rushing.
Yeah, that's true. I'll give it more space in the report, and maybe use an example from a particular city.
So what should I change for the written version?
Two things. First, I'd add a comparison. Look at how the Netherlands handled the same pressures – they made very different choices.
I was also thinking of interviewing some local cyclists.
It's a nice idea, but you'd need ethics approval, and there simply isn't time before the deadline.
Maybe save that for your dissertation next year.
OK. Should I put in more maps?
No, you've got plenty of maps. But your figures stop around 2010. You should update them with something more recent.
Fair enough. And the introduction's OK as it is?
The introduction's fine. Leave it.
Let's talk about your sources. What are you planning to do with each one?
Well, the transport museum website – some of its numbers don't match the books I used, so I'm going to double-check its figures.
Sensible. And the 1972 government report?
That's really my strongest source, so I'll build the main argument around it.
Good. What about the cycling club newsletter?
I thought about asking the librarian if there were other issues, but honestly, it's quite one-sided. I'm going to take it out altogether.
I think that's wise. And the documentary film?
It quoted a historian, Dr Weber, so I'm going to track down the article she originally wrote, instead of relying on the film.
Excellent. Always better to go back to the original. Right, I think you're in good shape.
When is the report due, exactly? I wrote down two different dates.
It's the end of next month. Send me a draft of the comparison section a week before, if you like, and I'll give you some quick comments.
That would be really helpful. Thanks so much, Dr Ellis.

listening.title: Sleep and memory in teenagers
listening.titleVi: Giấc ngủ và trí nhớ ở tuổi thiếu niên
listening.context: A university lecture on how sleep affects memory consolidation in teenagers.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about sleep and memory in teenagers. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're looking at something that affects every one of you: sleep, and in particular how it shapes memory in adolescence.
I'll start with the basic process, then look at what's different about teenagers, then a recent study, and finally what all this means in practice.
So, first, memory consolidation. That's the process by which fragile, short-term memories become stable, long-term ones.
For a long time, sleep was seen as a passive state – the brain simply switching off. We now know that's wrong.
In fact, some areas of the brain are almost as active during certain stages of sleep as they are when we're awake.
During sleep, the brain essentially replays the day's experiences, running through the same patterns of activity again and again.
The key structure here is the hippocampus, a small, curved region deep in the brain.
You can think of it as a temporary store, a kind of inbox, where new information is held for a short time.
Then, during deep sleep, that information is gradually transferred to the cortex, the outer layer of the brain, for long-term storage.
What about REM sleep, the stage when we dream? Its role is less clear. It doesn't seem to be essential for storing facts.
But it may help with creative thinking – making unexpected connections between ideas we already have.
In several experiments, people who'd had a period of REM sleep were better at solving puzzles that needed a fresh approach.
OK, so why are teenagers a special case? Well, it's not simply that they're lazy, whatever their parents might say.
At puberty, the body clock shifts. In particular, the release of melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, is delayed by up to two hours.
Screens and phone use make this worse, but they're not the root cause. The shift is biological.
The result is that a typical sixteen-year-old simply isn't tired at ten o'clock, yet still has to get up at six thirty for school.
Over a week, that builds up into what researchers call sleep debt, and it's very hard to pay back at the weekend.
And how much sleep do teenagers actually need? Many parents believe seven hours is enough.
In fact, the research suggests roughly nine hours a night – and very few teenagers get anywhere near that during the school week.
Let's turn now to a study I want to describe in some detail. Researchers worked with two hundred students aged fifteen to seventeen.
Each student learned forty words from an invented language – invented, so that nobody could have seen the words before.
Half of them learned the words in the evening and then slept. The other half learned them in the morning and stayed awake all day.
Importantly, both groups had the same amount of time to study, and they used exactly the same materials.
Twelve hours later, both groups were tested. The early analysis suggested the sleep group remembered about thirty percent more.
But once the researchers removed students who'd reported being ill, the difference settled at twenty percent. Still a very substantial effect.
The researchers also found that the benefit was greatest for the words students had found most difficult during learning.
In other words, sleep seemed to help most with the information that was weakest to begin with.
So, finally, what are the practical implications?
At the level of policy, several districts have experimented with starting the school day later, around eight thirty instead of seven thirty.
Schools that made the change generally reported fewer absences, and in some cases, modest improvements in grades.
There were concerns that students would just go to bed later, but most of the data shows they actually gained around forty minutes of sleep.
Of course, a later start creates problems too, with buses, sports schedules and parents' working hours, so it isn't an easy decision.
And for individual students, the message is simple. Probably the worst thing you can do before an exam is late-night cramming.
You may feel you're gaining time, but you're cutting out the very sleep your brain needs to keep what you've studied.
A far better strategy is to spread your revision over several days, and let each night of sleep do some of the work for you.
Right. Next week we'll look at how exercise affects attention.

readings.title: The Rise of Urban Farming
readings.summaryVi: Nông nghiệp đô thị đang phát triển ở nhiều thành phố, mang lại thực phẩm tươi và lợi ích xã hội nhưng vẫn gặp khó khăn về chi phí và đất đai.
readings.summaryEn: Urban farming is growing in many cities, bringing fresh food and social benefits, but it still struggles with costs and a lack of land.
readings.text:
For most of history, food was grown in the countryside and carried into towns. Today, however, a growing number of people are producing fruit and vegetables inside cities. This practice, known as urban farming, can take many forms, from small gardens on rooftops to large indoor farms in old warehouses.

One reason for its popularity is the wish to eat fresh, local food. When vegetables are grown close to where people live, they do not need to travel long distances by lorry or plane. Supporters argue that this can reduce pollution and help cities become more sustainable. In addition, food that is picked on the same day it is sold often tastes better and keeps more of its nutrients.

Urban farms also bring social benefits. In many neighbourhoods, community gardens give residents a place to meet, share skills and spend time outdoors. Teachers sometimes use school gardens to show children where their food comes from, and some studies suggest that young people who take part are more willing to try new vegetables. For older residents, gardening can be a gentle form of exercise.

Nevertheless, urban farming faces several challenges. Land in cities is expensive, so farmers may struggle to find suitable space. Indoor farms, which use artificial light instead of sunlight, can consume a great deal of electricity. As a result, the yield from these farms must be high enough to cover their costs. Soil in some urban areas may also contain harmful substances left by old factories, which means it has to be tested carefully before anything is planted.

Despite these problems, many experts believe that urban farming will continue to expand. It is unlikely to replace traditional agriculture completely, but it could become an important supplement, especially in crowded cities where fresh produce is hard to find.

questions.q: Urban farming only takes place on the roofs of buildings.
questions.explain: Bài nói nông nghiệp đô thị có nhiều dạng "from small gardens on rooftops to large indoor farms in old warehouses", không chỉ trên mái nhà → FALSE.

questions.q: Vegetables picked on the day they are sold may contain more nutrients.
questions.explain: Bài viết: food picked on the same day "often tastes better and keeps more of its nutrients" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most city governments provide free land for community gardens.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói đất đô thị đắt ("Land in cities is expensive"), không đề cập chính quyền cấp đất miễn phí → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might soil in some urban areas need to be tested?
options: It may contain harmful substances from old factories.
It is too expensive to buy.
questions.explain: Bài viết: soil "may also contain harmful substances left by old factories".

questions.q: What do many experts think about the future of urban farming?
options: It will completely replace traditional agriculture.
It will soon disappear because of high costs.
It will grow and act as a supplement to traditional farming.
It will only be found in schools.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "unlikely to replace traditional agriculture completely, but it could become an important supplement".

readings.title: The Four-Day Working Week
readings.summaryVi: Tuần làm việc bốn ngày được thử nghiệm ở nhiều nơi; kết quả ban đầu khả quan về năng suất và sức khỏe, nhưng không phù hợp với mọi ngành.
readings.summaryEn: The four-day working week has been tested in many places; early results for productivity and well-being are promising, but it does not suit every industry.
readings.text:
The idea that people should work five days a week is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a relatively recent invention. In the early twentieth century, many factory workers laboured for six days, and the two-day weekend was only gradually adopted. Today, a new proposal is attracting attention: reducing the standard week to four days without cutting pay.

Advocates of the four-day week claim that it can boost productivity rather than reduce it. Their reasoning is that employees who are well rested tend to concentrate better and waste less time. Trials carried out by companies and researchers in several countries have reported encouraging results, with many participating firms stating that output remained stable while staff reported lower levels of stress and burnout. Some organisations also found it easier to recruit and retain skilled workers, as the shorter week was seen as an attractive benefit.

However, critics point out that these trials have limitations. Most of the businesses involved volunteered to take part, which suggests they may have been particularly well suited to the change. In addition, the findings often rely on self-reported data, which can be influenced by participants' enthusiasm for the scheme. It is therefore difficult to know whether the same outcomes would be achieved across the wider economy.

Certain sectors face particular obstacles. Hospitals, schools and public transport, for example, must provide services every day, so a reduced week would require more staff or complex rotas. In such cases, the cost of implementation could be considerable. Small businesses with only a handful of employees may also struggle to cover absences.

For these reasons, many analysts expect a gradual and uneven shift rather than a sudden transformation. Some companies may adopt a full four-day week, while others experiment with flexible arrangements, such as compressed hours or reduced Friday shifts. Whatever form it takes, the debate reflects a broader question about how societies balance economic growth with wellbeing.

questions.q: The two-day weekend was introduced suddenly in the early twentieth century.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói cuối tuần hai ngày "was only gradually adopted" (được áp dụng dần dần), không phải đột ngột → FALSE.

questions.q: Some organisations in the trials found it easier to keep skilled staff.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Some organisations also found it easier to recruit and retain skilled workers" → TRUE.

questions.q: Employees in the trials were required to work longer hours on the remaining four days.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nhắc "compressed hours" như một lựa chọn trong tương lai, không nói người tham gia thử nghiệm phải làm thêm giờ → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do critics doubt the trial results?
options: The trials lasted only a few days.
Participating companies volunteered and data were often self-reported.
Workers were paid less during the trials.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Most of the businesses involved volunteered" và "findings often rely on self-reported data".

questions.q: According to the passage, why might hospitals find a four-day week difficult?
questions.explain: Bài viết: hospitals, schools and public transport "must provide services every day".

readings.title: Microplastics in the Ocean
readings.summaryVi: Vi nhựa xuất hiện khắp đại dương từ nhiều nguồn khác nhau; tác động lâu dài còn chưa rõ và cần giải pháp từ gốc.
readings.summaryEn: Microplastics now appear throughout the oceans from many different sources; their long-term effects are still unclear, and solutions must tackle the problem at its source.
readings.text:
Plastic has transformed modern life, but its durability has created a serious environmental problem. Once plastic reaches the sea, it does not simply disappear. Instead, sunlight, waves and changes in temperature gradually break it into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces less than five millimetres across are known as microplastics, and scientists now detect them in almost every marine environment they examine, from coastal waters to the deep ocean floor.

Microplastics come from a variety of sources. Some are the result of larger items, such as bottles and fishing nets, breaking down over time. Others are released directly in tiny form. Synthetic clothing, for instance, can shed fibres when it is washed, and these may pass through water treatment systems and eventually flow into rivers and seas. Vehicle tyres also wear away on roads, producing particles that are carried by rainwater into drainage systems.

The consequences for marine life are a cause of growing concern. Small animals such as plankton and shellfish can mistake microplastics for food. Researchers worry that the particles may accumulate as they move up the food chain, potentially affecting larger fish and, ultimately, humans who eat seafood. Laboratory studies suggest that some organisms grow more slowly when exposed to high concentrations, although it remains unclear whether similar effects occur in natural conditions.

Tackling the problem is complicated because microplastics are extremely difficult to remove once they are dispersed in the water. Cleaning the open ocean on a large scale is generally considered impractical. Consequently, many experts argue that prevention is more effective than cure. Proposed measures include improving waste management, designing washing machines with better filters, and encouraging manufacturers to use materials that degrade more safely.

Ultimately, the issue highlights the hidden costs of convenience. Reducing microplastic pollution will require cooperation between governments, industry and consumers, as well as further research into the long-term effects on ecosystems.

questions.explain: Bài viết: "Cleaning the open ocean on a large scale is generally considered impractical. Consequently... prevention is more effective".

readings.title: How Sleep Affects Memory
readings.summaryVi: Giấc ngủ giúp não củng cố trí nhớ; thiếu ngủ làm giảm khả năng học tập, nên học sinh không nên thức khuya ôn bài.
readings.summaryEn: Sleep helps the brain consolidate memories; lack of sleep reduces the ability to learn, so students should not stay up late to revise.
readings.text:
Many students believe that staying up late to study is the best way to prepare for an exam. However, scientists who study the brain increasingly suggest that this habit may do more harm than good. Sleep, it seems, plays an essential role in helping us remember what we have learned.

When we learn something new, the information is first stored in a temporary form. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and organise these new memories, moving them into longer-term storage. This process is often called consolidation. Researchers believe that different stages of sleep may support different types of memory. For example, deep sleep may help us remember facts, while the dreaming stage may be linked to skills and creative thinking.

Experiments in several countries have compared people who slept after learning with people who stayed awake. In many of these studies, the participants who slept were better at recalling the information later. Some research also suggests that a short nap during the day can improve performance on simple memory tasks, although the benefits of napping may depend on its length and timing.

A lack of sleep, on the other hand, can make learning more difficult. People who are tired often find it hard to concentrate, and they may feel irritable or anxious. Over time, regular sleep deprivation has been associated with a range of health problems, which can further affect a person's ability to study and work effectively.

So what can learners do? Experts generally recommend keeping a regular routine, going to bed and waking up at similar times each day. They also advise avoiding bright screens late in the evening, as the light may make it harder to fall asleep. Rather than studying all night before an exam, students might achieve better results by reviewing their notes earlier and then getting a full night's rest.

questions.q: New information is first stored in the brain in a temporary form.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the information is first stored in a temporary form" → TRUE.

questions.explain: Bài viết nói lợi ích của ngủ trưa "may depend on its length and timing", nên không phải mọi giấc ngủ trưa đều có ích → FALSE.

questions.explain: Bài không đề cập thời điểm học ưa thích của những người ngủ đủ giấc → NOT GIVEN.

questions.explain: Bài viết: "deep sleep may help us remember facts".

options: The light may make it harder to fall asleep.
They reduce the time for studying.
They cause people to forget facts.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the light may make it harder to fall asleep".

readings.title: The Silent Loss of Languages
readings.summaryVi: Nhiều ngôn ngữ đang biến mất do áp lực kinh tế và xã hội; mất ngôn ngữ là mất tri thức văn hóa, và nỗ lực phục hồi cần cộng đồng chủ động tham gia.
readings.summaryEn: Many languages are disappearing under economic and social pressure; losing a language means losing cultural knowledge, and revival efforts need communities to take an active part.
readings.text:
Linguists broadly agree that a substantial proportion of the world's languages are at risk of disappearing within the coming generations. Unlike the extinction of a plant or animal species, however, the loss of a language rarely attracts headlines. It tends to occur quietly, as each successive generation uses the ancestral tongue a little less until, eventually, no fluent speakers remain.

The forces driving this decline are rarely a matter of deliberate prohibition alone, although historical policies of forced assimilation have certainly played a part in many regions. More commonly, the shift is propelled by economic and social pressures. Parents who perceive a dominant language as the key to education and employment may choose not to pass on their own, believing they are acting in their children's best interests. Urban migration, mass media and the internet can accelerate this process by exposing young people predominantly to a handful of global languages.

Why should such losses matter? One argument is that each language encodes a distinctive way of categorising experience. Vocabulary relating to local plants, weather patterns or kinship structures may embody knowledge accumulated over centuries, some of which is not documented anywhere else. When a language vanishes, this intangible heritage may disappear with it. Moreover, for many communities, language is inseparable from identity, and its erosion can be experienced as a profound cultural dislocation.

Efforts at revitalisation have produced mixed outcomes. Documentation projects, in which researchers record speakers and compile dictionaries, preserve valuable material but do not in themselves create new speakers. More ambitious initiatives, such as immersion schools where children are taught entirely in the endangered language, have reportedly achieved notable success in certain contexts. Nevertheless, such programmes demand sustained funding and, crucially, the commitment of the community itself.

The prevailing view among specialists is that external intervention can support, but never substitute for, local motivation. A language survives not because it is archived, but because people continue to choose to speak it in their daily lives.

questions.explain: Bài viết: the loss of a language "rarely attracts headlines", trái với ý của câu → FALSE.

questions.q: Some parents stop passing on their language because they think it will help their children.
questions.explain: Bài viết: parents may choose not to pass on their own, "believing they are acting in their children's best interests" → TRUE.

questions.q: Immersion schools are cheaper to run than documentation projects.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói trường immersion "demand sustained funding", không so sánh chi phí với dự án ghi chép → NOT GIVEN.

options: They do not in themselves create new speakers.
questions.explain: Bài viết: documentation projects "preserve valuable material but do not in themselves create new speakers".

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Archiving is the most effective way to save a language.
Global languages should be taught less in schools.
A language survives only if people keep choosing to use it.
questions.explain: Câu cuối: "A language survives not because it is archived, but because people continue to choose to speak it".

readings.title: Why We Throw Away So Much Food
readings.summaryVi: Khoảng một phần ba lượng thực phẩm trên thế giới bị bỏ phí; bài viết giải thích nguyên nhân, tác hại với môi trường và những thói quen nhỏ giúp giảm lãng phí.
readings.summaryEn: About a third of the world's food is wasted; the article explains the causes, the harm to the environment and the small habits that help reduce waste.
readings.text:
Every year, people around the world throw away a huge amount of food. Experts say that about one third of all the food we produce is never eaten. Some of it is lost on farms or during transport, but a large part is wasted in our own homes.

Why does this happen? One common reason is that people buy too much. When food is on special offer in the supermarket, it is easy to fill the basket with more than we need. Another reason is confusion about the dates on packets. Many people think that food must go in the bin after its "best before" date, but this date is only about quality, not safety. Food is often still good to eat after it.

Food waste is also a problem for the environment. When old food goes to a landfill, it slowly breaks down and produces gases that make the planet warmer. In addition, a lot of water, energy and land was used to grow the food in the first place, so all of these resources are wasted too.

The good news is that small changes can help. Before going shopping, you can check your fridge and write a list. You can keep leftovers in a box and eat them the next day. Some families freeze bread and fruit so that they last longer. In several countries, there are now apps that let shops and cafés sell unsold meals cheaply at the end of the day.

If everyone wasted a little less, the total amount would fall a lot. And there is one more reason to try: saving food also means saving money.

questions.explain: Bài viết: "about one third of all the food we produce is never eaten" → TRUE.

questions.explain: Bài viết nói ngày "best before" chỉ liên quan đến chất lượng: "this date is only about quality, not safety" → FALSE.

questions.explain: Bài viết: "When food is on special offer in the supermarket, it is easy to fill the basket with more than we need".
